plays.play: Using an address Ada passed along anonymously, Tommy offers Campbell a bigger prize: a senior Communist holding £200 in cash from the Russian government, a catch that could win Campbell proof of a conspiracy and perhaps a medal. Before handing over the address, he asks for Campbell's word that Freddie and Ada can leave the city, and Campbell gives it.
plays.why_it_works: Substituting a more valuable prize for the one demanded should let both sides claim a win: Campbell's career gets a boost and Ada is protected.
plays.outcome: It fails twice. Campbell breaks his word the moment the man is arrested and has him brutally interrogated for Freddie's whereabouts, and the prize turns out to be worthless, because the comrades do not know each other's addresses. The prisoner dies, Freddie is arrested at his son's birth, and the family blames Tommy.
plays.counter: Tommy needed an enforceable guarantee, such as holding back the stolen guns Campbell was desperate to recover until Freddie and Ada were clear, instead of the word of a man who openly despised him. He should also have checked whether the asset he traded could deliver what Campbell wanted.
plays.principle: A promise from someone who holds you in contempt is worth nothing unless something enforces it.
plays.in_practice: When a counterparty has shown they will not honor informal commitments, put terms in writing with consequences, or make delivery simultaneous. And confirm that what you are trading actually has the value you claim.

quote.text: My word to who? To a Peaky Blinder?
quote.speaker: Inspector Campbell

plays.title: Surrender Without a Guarantee
plays.context: Lagertha, Ragnar's first wife and now a formidable warlord, has seized Kattegat while Ragnar is away. Queen Aslaug, Ragnar's second wife, who has ruled in his absence, has no force left to resist.
plays.play: Aslaug opens by calling Lagertha a usurper, then plants doubt by claiming she dreamed that Ragnar and her son Ivar drowned. She says she has no wish to fight, since she would never win, claims her place in Ragnar's saga through her sons, and asks only for safe passage. She offers Lagertha her hearth and home with her blessing, and adds a sweetener: her sons will be grateful for the manner of it and will not seek revenge. Lagertha says she understands, and as Aslaug walks away, shoots her with an arrow.
plays.why_it_works: Aslaug correctly identifies what Lagertha fears, a revenge war with Ragnar's sons, and tries to trade it away. It fails because she is promising something she cannot enforce on behalf of people who are not in the room, and killing her costs Lagertha almost nothing.
plays.outcome: Aslaug dies. Her son Ivar returns demanding vengeance, and the feud she tried to prevent becomes the main threat to Lagertha's rule.
plays.counter: Aslaug needed something Lagertha valued that only a living Aslaug could deliver, or a witness who would enforce the deal, before she gave up the hall.
plays.principle: A surrender that relies on the other side's goodwill is no deal: bring something they lose by breaking it.
plays.in_practice: When you negotiate from weakness, do not hand over your last asset for a verbal promise. Tie their benefit to a later step that only you can complete.

quote.text: And my sons, when they hear how it was done, will be grateful for the manner of it... And not seek revenge.
quote.speaker: Aslaug

plays.title: The Revised Promise
plays.target: Marty Spinella and the teachers' unions
plays.context: Frank, then House Majority Whip, must deliver the new President's education bill, with performance standards for teachers, over the opposition of the teachers' unions and their chief lobbyist, Marty Spinella. Called away to his home district, he negotiates by phone and concedes too much, including testing only every five years.
plays.play: Frank quietly adds a provision threatening federal funds for school districts with collective bargaining, meaning to trade it away later to win back performance standards. He shows Spinella a version without it. When a colleague calls this lying, Frank says he revised the parameters of his promise. When Spinella finds the clause, Frank tells him it was only there for leverage and asks to reopen performance standards.
plays.why_it_works: An extreme demand you are ready to drop can be traded for what you really want, and adding it late gets around earlier concessions. The same move destroys trust once the other side learns it was hidden from them.
plays.outcome: It backfires. Spinella calls it a dirty bomb, declares war and leads a nationwide teachers' strike. Frank has to resort to much dirtier tricks, including goading Spinella into hitting him, to win the fight back, and reflects that friends make the worst enemies.
plays.counter: Spinella should have insisted on a signed text of the agreed points before his people left the room. Frank's own mistake was leaving the table; as Spinella tells him, he should have been there in person.
plays.principle: A bargaining chip hidden from your counterpart becomes a betrayal the moment they find it.
plays.in_practice: Anchoring high is legitimate when it is out in the open; slipping new terms into a draft after agreement burns the relationship. Stay at the table in person for the critical rounds.

quote.text: No. I revised the parameters of my promise.
quote.speaker: Frank Underwood

plays.title: One More Thing
plays.target: Logan Sanders; Linda Johnson, a landlord's attorney
plays.context: Twice, Mike wins a negotiation and then loses it at the close. In the first, now an investment banker fighting for control of a company, he has Logan Sanders, the rival bidder and Harvey's client, agreeing to buy him out on generous terms. In the second, out of prison and working at a legal clinic, he has pressured a landlord's lawyer into settling a tenant's claim after her child was hurt in an illegal demolition.
plays.play: With Logan, after agreeing a generous number paid up front, Mike adds a surprise condition suggested by his girlfriend Rachel, who wants Logan gone for her own reasons: once the deal is done, Harvey goes back to being Mike's lawyer and Logan is out. Logan suggests Harvey choose; Harvey picks Mike, and Logan walks away from the terms he has just agreed. At the clinic, Mike gets the landlord's lawyer, Linda Johnson, to name a number, guesses her authority ('you're authorized to go to 20, so let's say 25') and closes at $25,000. When his client learns her son's treatment costs that much every year, Mike goes back the same night and demands $100,000. Johnson calls it bad faith, says his client is running him, and goes to trial.
plays.why_it_works: Both negotiations work until the extra demand. A surprise condition at the close turns a commercial deal into a contest of pride, and reopening a settled number destroys credibility and tells the other side you cannot control your own client.
plays.outcome: The settlement dies and Mike loses the company fight to Logan. At trial Johnson exploits the clinic's weak point, that Mike is not a lawyer and the colleague arguing the case freezes, and the case is dismissed with prejudice. The client gets nothing.
plays.counter: Harvey's verdict on the first: Mike had leverage and wanted to be sure Logan knew it, when he should have raised the side issue with Harvey privately. For the second, Mike needed to agree his client's walk-away number before he negotiated, so the first yes would hold.
plays.principle: Once you have won, sign; one more demand turns a deal into a fight over pride.
plays.in_practice: When a negotiation reaches agreement, close it, and handle side issues separately and privately. Before you negotiate for a client or your own firm, agree what yes looks like, because going back for more after a handshake usually loses the deal.

quote.text: You should have come to me first Instead of looking to rub it in his face.
quote.speaker: Harvey Specter
